blocks.text: By the end of the week, Jenny could scarcely walk past a shop window without seeing Eleanor Blackwell’s name. FREE ELECTRICITY appeared beneath it on handbills, posters and a sign outside the meeting hall.
Her editor dropped a clipping beside her typewriter. “People are asking when it starts.”
“If she wins,” Jenny said. “That’s the only date she’s given us.”
“Then find out what happens before that. Who’s building it? Where’s the demonstration?” He tapped the clipping. “We’ve printed the promise. I want the details.”
Jenny took out her notebook. She already had a page of questions. None had become easier since the rooftop conversation.
Eleanor’s aide tried to offer another campaign statement. Jenny asked for Eleanor herself. After a long wait, a cooler voice came onto the line.
“Miss Jenkins. I believe I answered your questions at the meeting.”
“You said the technical work was being handled. I’d like to interview the person handling it.”
“The work isn’t ready for public inspection.”
“An interview doesn’t have to be a public inspection. Who’s the scientist, and when will there be something people can see?”
Eleanor said nothing. Jenny heard papers moving at the other end.
“I can report that you declined,” Jenny added. “But I’d rather give readers an answer.”
“You reporters do enjoy making everything sound sinister.”
“Free electricity is a large promise. People want to know how you’ll keep it.”
Another pause. Then Eleanor said, “I’ll see what can be arranged.”
Jenny wrote those words beneath the unanswered questions. “Thank you. You can reach me at the newsroom.”
Eleanor waited until the line was clear before making her next call.
Daniel answered on the sixth ring. Something clattered behind him.
“What was that?” she asked.
“Nothing important.”
“You need to give me something I can show people. Soon. They’re starting to ask for more than speeches.”
“Skyfall needs time.”
“And Jenny Jenkins needs a story. She wants to interview the scientist.”
Daniel pulled the newspaper out from beneath his notes. “Does she?”
“She keeps asking questions. You can be sure Billy is somewhere behind her.” Eleanor lowered her voice. “I will not have your name turn this campaign into a discussion of that robot.”
Daniel smiled down at the byline. “Then let me show her something else.”
blocks.alt: Eleanor speaks sternly on the telephone from her campaign office while Daniel takes the call in his cluttered laboratory, with Luke’s floating head and iron jaws watching uneasily.

blocks.text: “What, exactly?”
“A private demonstration. Just the reporter. I can explain the principle without opening the workshop to a crowd.”
Eleanor considered it. “Can you make it convincing?”
“I can make sure she has plenty to write about.”
“Keep it about electricity, Daniel. And clean the place first.”
He looked around the bench. “Of course.”
Luke waited until his uncle put the receiver down. He had heard enough of the call to recognize the name.
“The reporter from the newspaper?”
Daniel turned the page toward him. “The very same.”
Luke looked from the byline to the photograph of Zerdo. “You’re bringing her here?”
“She wants to ask a few questions.”
“And you’re going to answer them?”
“Some of them.” Daniel drew a line beneath the reporter’s name, then reached for a clean sheet of paper.
Luke drifted closer. “You think Zerdo will just walk in after her?”
Daniel’s pencil stopped. He looked up through his enormous glasses.
“If Billy asks for help,” Daniel said. “He works with them. When his reporter friend doesn’t come back, who do you think he’ll send?”
Luke looked at the byline again. To him, Jenny Jenkins was a reporter who had written about Zerdo. Neither he nor Daniel knew she was the pink blur.

Luke glanced toward the rear workshop. The collector stood unfinished behind a tangle of cables. There was still no body waiting for him. Just his uncle’s promises and another person about to trust one of them.
“The collector isn’t finished,” Luke said. “Why are we trying to catch him now?”
“Because a body like his may not come through that door twice,” Daniel said. “First I secure him. Then the fireball’s energy and the rest of the equipment.”
“Does she know what you did?” he asked.
“She was at the lake with Billy. She’s seen the equipment. And she wrote the story about the robot.”
“That might be enough to keep her away.”
“Then we’ll have to give her a good reason to come.” Daniel began writing.

The invitation reached the newsroom the following afternoon. Eleanor’s office offered Jenny an exclusive interview and a small-scale demonstration of the proposed electricity system. An address and appointment time were typed at the bottom, followed by directions to the basement service entrance through the sunken yard.
Jenny read it twice, then took it to Billy. In his office, she shut the door before handing it over.
blocks.alt: Civilian reporter Jenny reads the laboratory invitation at Billy’s office desk while Billy checks his appointment notebook beside her.

blocks.text: He read it once. “That was quick.”
“I asked to meet the scientist. Apparently, she’s decided I can.”
“Apparently.” He laid the paper flat on his desk. “Who’s expecting you?”
“Her office says the project’s technical adviser. No name, but that’s Daniel’s building. This says to go downstairs.”
Billy’s eyes narrowed. “So she’s sending you straight back to him. Jenny, he’s already endangered people. An invitation from her campaign doesn’t make him safe.”
“This is the access we’ve been asking for,” Jenny said. “I’ll go openly, as a reporter, and write down what he shows me. If he turns threatening, I trust my feet to get me out.”
Billy opened his notebook. “Leave me the address and the appointment time. Call me an hour after you get there. If the interview runs longer, let me know before that hour’s up.”
Jenny nodded. “I’ll call.”
“And I want you back with the answers.”
She copied the details into his notebook. For the first time since Eleanor’s speech, there was more on the page than a promise.
Across the city, Daniel cleared a space on the workbench. He folded the newspaper so that Jenny’s name stayed visible and set it beside the telephone.
